prompt: How does the section recommend working a synthesis problem for a substituted benzene?

choices.text: Backward (retrosynthetically), repeatedly asking “What is an immediate precursor of this compound?”
Forward from benzene, trying each available reaction until the target appears
choices.why: The section recommends the opposite: start from the target and work backward one step at a time.

choices.text: By always putting the most strongly activating group on first
choices.why: There is no such fixed rule; the right order depends on the directing effects needed, found by working backward.

choices.text: By choosing reactions that introduce all the substituents in a single step
choices.why: Substituents are introduced one at a time, and the order is often critical. The section plans backward from the target.

explanation: As in Section 9.9, it's usually best to work a synthesis problem backward, or retrosynthetically. Look at the target and ask, “What is an immediate precursor of this compound?” Choose a likely answer and keep working backward, one step at a time, until you reach a simple starting material.

prompt: Why is planning the order of reactions especially important when synthesizing substituted aromatic rings?

choices.text: Groups already on the ring direct where each new substituent goes
Each new substituent always goes para to the one added just before it
choices.why: Where a new group goes depends on whether the groups already present are ortho/para or meta directors, and on their strength.

choices.text: All aromatic substitutions are reversible, so later steps undo earlier ones
choices.why: Of the reactions in this chapter, sulfonation is the one described as readily reversible. The order matters because of directing effects.

choices.text: Substituents move around the ring if they are added in the wrong order
choices.why: Substituents stay where they are put. The order matters because each group directs where the next one goes.

explanation: The ability to plan a sequence of reactions in the right order is particularly important in the synthesis of substituted aromatic rings, where the introduction of a new substituent is strongly affected by the directing effects of other substituents. Some reactions, such as Friedel–Crafts reactions, also fail once certain groups are on the ring.

prompt: In planning a synthesis of 4-bromo-2-nitrotoluene from benzene, which final step gives the target as a single product?

choices.text: Nitration of p-bromotoluene
Bromination of o-nitrotoluene
choices.why: The activating methyl group would direct bromine to the correct position, but a mixture of product isomers would form.

choices.text: Friedel–Crafts methylation of m-bromonitrobenzene
choices.why: Friedel–Crafts reactions don't work on a nitro-substituted (strongly deactivated) ring.

choices.text: Bromination of p-nitrotoluene
choices.why: Both groups of p-nitrotoluene direct bromine ortho to the methyl group, giving 2-bromo-4-nitrotoluene, a different compound.

explanation: Worked Example 16.10.1: the best immediate precursor is p-bromotoluene, which is nitrated ortho to the activating methyl group to give a single product. Bromination of o-nitrotoluene would give a mixture, and a Friedel–Crafts reaction can't be the last step because it fails on a nitro-substituted ring.

prompt: Which sequence converts benzene into 4-bromo-2-nitrotoluene?

choices.text: 1. CH3Cl, AlCl3; 2. Br2, FeBr3, keeping the para isomer; 3. HNO3, H2SO4
1. HNO3, H2SO4; 2. CH3Cl, AlCl3; 3. Br2, FeBr3
choices.why: Friedel–Crafts methylation fails on nitrobenzene, a strongly deactivated ring.

choices.text: 1. Br2, FeBr3; 2. HNO3, H2SO4; 3. CH3Cl, AlCl3
choices.why: The Friedel–Crafts step comes last, on a nitro-substituted ring, where it doesn't work.

choices.text: 1. CH3Cl, AlCl3; 2. HNO3, H2SO4, keeping the para isomer; 3. Br2, FeBr3
choices.why: p-Nitrotoluene is brominated ortho to the methyl group, giving 2-bromo-4-nitrotoluene, not the target.

explanation: Methylating benzene gives toluene, and bromination gives o- and p-bromotoluene, which must be separated. Nitration of p-bromotoluene ortho to the activating methyl group then gives 4-bromo-2-nitrotoluene. Brominating first and then methylating is the other valid way to reach p-bromotoluene.

prompt: How many reaction steps does the book's route from benzene to 4-bromo-2-nitrotoluene have?
explanation: Worked Example 16.10.1 introduces each of the three substituents in its own step: methylation (CH3Cl, AlCl3) and bromination (Br2, FeBr3), in either order, give p-bromotoluene, and nitration (HNO3, H2SO4) comes last. That is three steps.

prompt: The retrosynthetic analysis finds two ways to make p-bromotoluene from benzene. Which statement about them is correct?

choices.text: Both methylating bromobenzene and brominating toluene work, but each gives an ortho/para mixture
Only bromination of toluene works, because Friedel–Crafts methylation fails on bromobenzene
choices.why: The book calls both routes satisfactory; methylating bromobenzene gives a mixture of ortho and para products.

choices.text: Both routes give pure p-bromotoluene, with no ortho isomer to separate
choices.why: Both methyl and bromine are ortho and para directors, so both routes unavoidably give mixtures to separate.

choices.text: Both routes give mainly m-bromotoluene, because bromine is deactivating
choices.why: Bromine deactivates the ring but is an ortho and para director, so the products are ortho and para.

explanation: Toluene is a possible precursor because the methyl group directs bromination ortho and para. Bromobenzene is another, because Friedel–Crafts methylation gives a mixture of ortho and para products. Both answers are satisfactory, although both lead unavoidably to a mixture of products that must be separated.

prompt: In the synthesis of 4-chloro-2-propylbenzenesulfonic acid, how is the propyl group put on the ring?

choices.text: Friedel–Crafts acylation with CH3CH2COCl and AlCl3, followed by reduction with H2/Pd
Friedel–Crafts alkylation with CH3CH2CH2Cl and AlCl3
choices.why: Primary alkyl groups such as propyl can't be introduced directly, because the carbocation rearranges.

choices.text: Friedel–Crafts alkylation with 2-chloropropane and AlCl3
choices.why: 2-Chloropropane gives an isopropyl group, not a propyl group.

choices.text: Friedel–Crafts acylation with CH3CH2COCl and AlCl3, followed by oxidation with KMnO4
choices.why: KMnO4 would oxidize the side chain to –CO2H. The C=O must be reduced to CH2 with H2 over Pd.

explanation: A propyl group can be introduced by Friedel–Crafts acylation with CH3CH2COCl/AlCl3 followed by reduction with H2/Pd. Direct alkylation with a primary alkyl halide gives carbocation rearrangement, and acyl cations don't rearrange.

prompt: Which final step does the retrosynthetic analysis choose for making 4-chloro-2-propylbenzenesulfonic acid?

choices.text: Sulfonation of m-chloropropylbenzene
Chlorination of o-propylbenzenesulfonic acid
choices.why: Both groups of o-propylbenzenesulfonic acid direct chlorine to other positions, so the reaction would occur at the wrong position.

choices.text: Friedel–Crafts introduction of the propyl group onto p-chlorobenzenesulfonic acid
choices.why: Friedel–Crafts reactions don't work on sulfonic-acid-substituted (strongly deactivated) rings.

choices.text: Sulfonation of p-chloropropylbenzene
choices.why: In the target, the chlorine is meta to the propyl group, not para, so p-chloropropylbenzene has the wrong substitution pattern.

explanation: Worked Example 16.10.2: chlorination of o-propylbenzenesulfonic acid would occur at the wrong position, and a Friedel–Crafts reaction fails on a sulfonic-acid-substituted ring. So the immediate precursor is m-chloropropylbenzene, which is sulfonated to give a mixture of isomers that must then be separated.

prompt: To make m-chloropropylbenzene from benzene, why is the acyl group put on before the chlorine?

choices.text: The first group must direct meta; an acyl group does, but chlorine directs ortho and para
Chlorine is a meta director, so it has to be the last group put on the ring
choices.why: Chlorine is an ortho and para director. That is exactly why it can't go on first: acylating chlorobenzene would not put the acyl group meta to it.

choices.text: The acyl group must be reduced to propyl before chlorination
choices.why: Reducing first would give propylbenzene, an ortho and para director, so chlorine would go to the wrong position. Reduction comes after chlorination.

choices.text: Chlorine must be added last because Cl2 and FeCl3 react with ketones
choices.why: The route chlorinates the ketone propiophenone in the ring, at the meta position, without trouble.

explanation: Because the two substituents have a meta relationship, the first substituent placed on the ring must be a meta director. Benzene is acylated to propiophenone, chlorinated meta to the acyl group to give m-chloropropiophenone, and then reduced to m-chloropropylbenzene.

prompt: Which sequence converts benzene into 4-chloro-2-propylbenzenesulfonic acid?

choices.text: 1. CH3CH2COCl, AlCl3; 2. Cl2, FeCl3; 3. H2/Pd; 4. SO3, H2SO4
1. CH3CH2COCl, AlCl3; 2. H2/Pd; 3. Cl2, FeCl3; 4. SO3, H2SO4
choices.why: Reducing first gives propylbenzene, whose propyl group directs chlorine ortho and para, not meta.

choices.text: 1. Cl2, FeCl3; 2. CH3CH2COCl, AlCl3; 3. H2/Pd; 4. SO3, H2SO4
choices.why: Chlorine is an ortho and para director, so the acyl group would not end up meta to it.

choices.text: 1. SO3, H2SO4; 2. CH3CH2COCl, AlCl3; 3. Cl2, FeCl3; 4. H2/Pd
choices.why: Friedel–Crafts acylation doesn't work on a sulfonic-acid-substituted (strongly deactivated) ring.

explanation: Worked Example 16.10.2 gives a four-step route: Friedel–Crafts acylation to propiophenone, chlorination meta to the acyl group, catalytic reduction to m-chloropropylbenzene, and sulfonation (the isomers are then separated).

prompt: How many steps does the book's route from benzene to 4-chloro-2-propylbenzenesulfonic acid have?
explanation: The final synthesis is a four-step route from benzene: acylation (CH3CH2COCl, AlCl3), chlorination (Cl2, FeCl3), hydrogenation (H2/Pd), and sulfonation (SO3, H2SO4). The propyl group alone takes two steps, acylation and reduction.

prompt: How would you make m-chloronitrobenzene from benzene?

choices.text: Nitrate first (HNO3, H2SO4), then chlorinate (Cl2, FeCl3)
Chlorinate first (Cl2, FeCl3), then nitrate (HNO3, H2SO4)
choices.why: Chlorine is an ortho and para director, so nitrating chlorobenzene gives mainly o- and p-chloronitrobenzene.

choices.text: Either order works equally well
choices.why: The order matters: only the meta-directing nitro group puts the second group meta.

choices.text: Neither order works, because a nitro group stops any further substitution
choices.why: A nitro ring can still be halogenated; for example, bromination of nitrobenzene gives m-bromonitrobenzene.

explanation: Exercise 16.10.1a: 1. HNO3, H2SO4; 2. Cl2, FeCl3. The nitro group is a meta director, so chlorinating nitrobenzene puts the chlorine meta to it.

prompt: Which sequence converts benzene into m-chloroethylbenzene?

choices.text: 1. CH3COCl, AlCl3; 2. Cl2, FeCl3; 3. H2/Pd
1. CH3CH2Cl, AlCl3; 2. Cl2, FeCl3
choices.why: An ethyl group is an ortho and para director, so chlorination would give o- and p-chloroethylbenzene.

choices.text: 1. Cl2, FeCl3; 2. CH3COCl, AlCl3; 3. H2/Pd
choices.why: Chlorine directs ortho and para, so the acetyl group would not end up meta to it.

choices.text: 1. CH3COCl, AlCl3; 2. H2/Pd; 3. Cl2, FeCl3
choices.why: Reducing first gives ethylbenzene, an ortho and para director, so the chlorine would go to the wrong positions.

explanation: Exercise 16.10.1b: acylation gives acetophenone, whose acetyl group directs chlorination meta. Catalytic hydrogenation over Pd then reduces the aryl ketone's C=O to CH2, turning the acetyl group into an ethyl group.

prompt: Which sequence converts benzene into 4-chloro-1-nitro-2-propylbenzene?

choices.text: 1. CH3CH2COCl, AlCl3; 2. Cl2, FeCl3; 3. H2/Pd; 4. HNO3, H2SO4
1. CH3CH2COCl, AlCl3; 2. Cl2, FeCl3; 3. HNO3, H2SO4; 4. H2/Pd
choices.why: Catalytic hydrogenation at the end would also reduce the nitro group to an amino group.

choices.text: 1. CH3CH2CH2Cl, AlCl3; 2. Cl2, FeCl3; 3. HNO3, H2SO4
choices.why: Alkylation with a primary halide rearranges, and a propyl group would direct chlorine ortho and para instead of meta.

choices.text: 1. HNO3, H2SO4; 2. CH3CH2COCl, AlCl3; 3. Cl2, FeCl3; 4. H2/Pd
choices.why: Friedel–Crafts acylation fails on nitrobenzene, a strongly deactivated ring.

explanation: Exercise 16.10.1c: acylation, then chlorination meta to the acyl group, then reduction to m-chloropropylbenzene, and finally nitration. The nitro group must go on last, because a nitro group is reduced to an amino group under H2/Pd conditions (Section 16.9).

prompt: In a route that uses both a ketone reduction with H2/Pd and an aromatic nitration, why must the nitration come after the hydrogenation?

choices.text: A nitro group on the ring would be reduced to an amino group by H2/Pd
Nitration would oxidize the alkyl side chain to a carboxylic acid
choices.why: Side-chain oxidation needs an oxidizing agent such as KMnO4. The problem is what H2/Pd does to a nitro group.

choices.text: H2/Pd reduces the aromatic ring when a nitro group is present
choices.why: Pd under ordinary conditions doesn't reduce the ring. It does reduce a nitro group to an amino group.

choices.text: The nitro group would rearrange to the meta position during hydrogenation
choices.why: Substituents don't move around the ring. The problem is that the nitro group itself is reduced.

explanation: Catalytic reduction of aryl alkyl ketones is not compatible with a nitro substituent on the ring, because a nitro group is reduced to an amino group under the reaction conditions; m-nitroacetophenone, for example, gives m-ethylaniline. So in routes such as Exercise 16.10.1c, the nitration is done after the H2/Pd step.

prompt: A planned synthesis starts with Friedel–Crafts acylation of benzonitrile, C6H5CN, using CH3COCl and AlCl3. What is wrong with this step?

choices.text: Friedel–Crafts acylation fails on a strongly deactivated ring
The acyl cation would rearrange before reacting
choices.why: Acyl cations are resonance-stabilized and don't rearrange. The problem is the deactivated ring.

choices.text: The ring would be acylated two or three times
choices.why: Acylations never occur more than once, and here the deactivated ring won't react at all.

choices.text: The acetyl group would go ortho and para to the –CN group
choices.why: –CN is a meta director, but the real problem is that the deactivated ring doesn't undergo Friedel–Crafts reactions.

explanation: Exercise 16.10.2a: Friedel–Crafts acylation does not occur on a deactivated ring. –CN is a strongly deactivating meta director, and Friedel–Crafts reactions don't succeed on rings with strongly electron-withdrawing groups.

prompt: A planned synthesis treats chlorobenzene with 1-chloropropane and AlCl3 to attach a propyl group. What goes wrong?

choices.text: The primary carbocation rearranges, so the ring gets isopropyl groups as well as propyl groups
Chlorobenzene is an aryl halide, so its ring can't be alkylated
choices.why: Aryl halides can't serve as the alkylating agent, but the chlorobenzene ring itself can be alkylated.

choices.text: 1-Chloropropane is a vinylic halide and doesn't react
choices.why: 1-Chloropropane is a primary alkyl halide. It reacts, but its carbocation rearranges.

choices.text: The chlorine on the ring deactivates it as strongly as a carbonyl group, so nothing happens
choices.why: Halogens are only weakly deactivating; the problem the book points out is rearrangement.

explanation: Exercise 16.10.2b: rearrangement occurs during Friedel–Crafts alkylation with primary halides, so a propyl group can't be introduced this way. Acylation with propanoyl chloride followed by H2/Pd reduction avoids the problem.

prompt: Using reactions from this chapter, which sequence converts benzene into m-bromobenzoic acid?

choices.text: 1. CH3Cl, AlCl3; 2. KMnO4, H2O; 3. Br2, FeBr3
1. CH3Cl, AlCl3; 2. Br2, FeBr3; 3. KMnO4, H2O
choices.why: Brominating toluene puts bromine ortho and para to the methyl group, so oxidation would give o- and p-bromobenzoic acid.

choices.text: 1. Br2, FeBr3; 2. CH3Cl, AlCl3; 3. KMnO4, H2O
choices.why: Bromine directs the methyl group ortho and para, so oxidation would give o- and p-bromobenzoic acid.

choices.text: 1. Br2, FeBr3; 2. KMnO4, H2O
choices.why: Bromobenzene has no alkyl side chain, and the ring itself is inert to KMnO4, so no carboxyl group forms.

explanation: Oxidizing toluene with KMnO4 gives benzoic acid. The –CO2H group is a meta director, so bromination then puts bromine meta to it. Brominating before oxidation would place bromine ortho or para, because the methyl group is an ortho and para director.

prompt: Which sequence converts benzene into m-nitroacetophenone?

choices.text: 1. CH3COCl, AlCl3; 2. HNO3, H2SO4
1. HNO3, H2SO4; 2. CH3COCl, AlCl3
choices.why: Friedel–Crafts acylation fails on nitrobenzene, a strongly deactivated ring.

choices.text: 1. CH3COCl, AlCl3; 2. HNO3, H2SO4; 3. H2/Pd
choices.why: The extra hydrogenation would reduce both the ketone and the nitro group, giving m-ethylaniline.

choices.text: 1. HNO3, H2SO4; 2. Fe, H3O+, then base; 3. CH3COCl, AlCl3
choices.why: Reduction gives aniline, and Friedel–Crafts reactions fail on rings with a basic amino group. The nitro group would also be gone.

explanation: Acylation of benzene gives acetophenone. The acetyl group is a meta director (nitration of the –COCH3 ring gives 72% meta product), so nitration then gives m-nitroacetophenone. Reversing the order fails because Friedel–Crafts reactions don't work on nitro-substituted rings.

prompt: Which sequence converts benzene into p-chloroacetophenone (after separating isomers where needed)?

choices.text: 1. Cl2, FeCl3; 2. CH3COCl, AlCl3, then separate the para isomer
1. CH3COCl, AlCl3; 2. Cl2, FeCl3
choices.why: The acetyl group is a meta director, so chlorination would give m-chloroacetophenone.

choices.text: 1. CH3COCl, AlCl3; 2. Cl2, FeCl3; 3. H2/Pd
choices.why: This puts the chlorine meta and then reduces the ketone, giving m-chloroethylbenzene.

choices.text: 1. Cl2, FeCl3; 2. CH3CH2Cl, AlCl3, then separate the para isomer
choices.why: Alkylation with chloroethane puts on an ethyl group, so the product has no C=O; it is p-chloroethylbenzene.

explanation: To get a para relationship, the first group must be an ortho and para director. Chlorine is one, so acylating chlorobenzene gives a mixture of ortho and para products from which p-chloroacetophenone is separated. Halogens are only weakly deactivating, so the ring still reacts, much as bromobenzene is methylated in Worked Example 16.10.1.
